subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98
textbook_items_in_class.description: Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball in India; (b) ages of dogs on this street; (c) fraction of the class who like walking up a hill; (d) do you like reading; (e) approximately how many bricks are in this wall; (f) best bowler in yesterday's match; (g) last year's rainfall pattern in Barmer.

time_bands.activity: Pose the guessing-from-height scenario from the chapter and ask students to raise hands for their guesses. Elicit: what information would help us be more certain? Introduce the idea that some questions can be answered by a single fact and others need gathered data to manage natural variation.

Present the statistical statement examples from section 13.1 — batting consistency, cycling time, village population — asking students to say, in each case, what numerical claim is being made and how someone might have arrived at it. Build a shared working definition: a statistical statement summarises a phenomenon using numbers, proportions, or predictions drawn from data.

Students work in pairs on Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98 (“Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball… (g) last year’s rainfall pattern in Barmer.”). Pairs share their reasoning for at least two items with the class and the class negotiates a joint verdict.

Bring together the pair decisions into a class list of statistical vs non-statistical questions. Name statistics as the study of collecting, organising, analysing, interpreting, and presenting data, and frame the chapter’s aim: using data and graphs to answer statistical questions.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who classify any question involving numbers as statistical — the key distinguishing feature is whether variation in answers is expected and whether data must be gathered to manage that variation. The guessing-gender-from-height example is a natural way to surface this: a single person’s height answers nothing, but the heights of many people reveal a pattern.

periods.activity_title: Arguing About What a Statement Really Claims

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98
textbook_items_in_class.description: Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball in India; (b) ages of dogs on this street; (c) fraction of the class who like walking up a hill; (d) do you like reading; (e) approximately how many bricks are in this wall; (f) best bowler in yesterday's match; (g) last year's rainfall pattern in Barmer.

time_bands.activity: Return to any Math Talk, section 13.1 p.98 (“Decide which of the following are statistical questions…”) items the class disagreed on. Each disagreeing pair states the full reasoning: does the question expect a single fixed answer or variation across observations? Use the chapter’s definition of a statistical question as the rule to apply.

In groups of three, students compose two of their own everyday questions — one statistical, one not — and write a one-sentence justification for each using the definition from section 13.1. Groups then exchange and challenge each other’s classification, citing the definition as authority.

Whole-class debrief: collect two or three contested pairs from the exchange. For each, the class applies the reasoning test — does answering it require collecting data from multiple sources because answers vary? Distinguish the role of the statistical question from the statistical statement that a completed study produces.
Quick consolidation: students write one statistical question they would genuinely like to investigate, keeping it for use as a reference point through the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is treating any question with a numerical answer as statistical — challenge this by offering ‘What is 7 × 8?’ and asking whether data must be collected. Encourage groups to use the chapter’s criterion of expected variation as a deductive rule rather than intuition.
materials: Blank index cards or slips of paper

periods.activity_title: Fair Shares and Averages in Real Data

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Shreyas bounces a ball on a bat with counts 6, 2, 9, 5, 4, 6, 3, 5 over 8 attempts; calculate the average number of bounces.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given weekly 100 m times for Nikhil (17, 18, 17, 16, 19, 17, 18) and Sunil (20, 18, 18, 17, 16, 16, 17), decide who on average ran quicker.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.101
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the mean enrolment given six years' figures 1555, 1670, 1750, 2013, 2040, 2126.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.2 p.101
homework.description: Collect your own bounce data for 7 or more attempts and find the average.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the cricket-comparison problem from section 13.2: two players, series of different lengths. Ask students: if you want to judge who is the better run-scorer, would you use the highest score, the total, or something else? Surface the problem that totals mislead when players played different numbers of matches.

Develop the arithmetic mean as fair-share using the guava-sharing and hibiscus-bloom examples from section 13.2. State the rule: mean = sum of values ÷ number of values. Mention the ancient Indian names for the mean (samamiti, samarajju, samīkaraṇa, sāmya) as recorded in the chapter. Students compute the mean for Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.101 (“Shreyas bounces a ball… 8 attempts”).

Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.101 (“Nikhil’s and Sunil’s 100 m times… decide who on average ran quicker”) and Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.101 (“Find the mean enrolment given six years’ figures”). Pairs record working clearly, noting sum and count separately.

Pairs share answers and reasoning. Discuss: when is the mean a fair representative value and when could it mislead? Connect back to the cricket example — a player with very few matches can show a high mean without sustained performance.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often divide by the wrong count — particularly when they include a zero value or accidentally count a repeated entry twice. Reinforce that every data point, including a zero, enters both the sum and the count. The fair-share image (redistribute guavas equally) is a useful correction: you cannot ignore any person in the sharing.
materials: Squared or plain paper for working

periods.activity_title: Dot Plots, Range, and the Onion-Price Story

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the median of the onion prices in Yahapur and in Wahapur.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: For Rintu's date-palm heights, fill the dot plot, mark the mean and median, describe the heights, find quicker ways to compute the mean, and count trees shorter than the average.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given daily water-usage values, (a) decide whether the mean or median can lie between 25 and 30, justifying using their meaning; (b) decide whether either can be less than the minimum or greater than the maximum value.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.2 p.112
homework.description: For Sanskruti's pet-count data (with some absent students), find the mean and median and describe the data.

time_bands.activity: Using the onion-price data for Yahapur and Wahapur from section 13.2, model the dot plot on the board: sort values, stack repeated values as dots above a number line. Students copy and complete the dot plot in their notebooks. Discuss what the dot plot reveals about clustering and spread that a plain list does not.

Introduce the median: the middle value of sorted data, or the average of the two middle values when there is an even count. Students find the median for Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.112 (“Find the median of the onion prices in Yahapur and in Wahapur”). Introduce outlier: a value that deviates greatly from the rest, and show how a low outlier pulls the mean below the median.

Students work in small groups on Figure it Out Q3, section 13.2 p.112 (“Rintu’s date-palm heights… fill the dot plot, mark the mean and median”) and Figure it Out Q4, section 13.2 p.112 (“Given daily water-usage values… decide whether the mean or median can lie between 25 and 30”). Groups reason aloud about the water-usage question before writing.

Groups report their reasoning for the water-usage question. Consolidate: name mean and median as measures of central tendency; name minimum, maximum, and range as descriptors of variability. Emphasise that both dimensions — centre and spread — are needed to describe a dataset.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the median position with a value they compute rather than locate. Reinforce the sort-then-locate procedure on the Rintu data: sort the values visually on the dot plot and physically point to the middle. Also watch for students who include absent students’ data in the count when computing medians — the chapter’s zero-versus-no-value distinction (a zero score vs not playing) should be raised explicitly.

periods.activity_title: When Mean and Median Tell Different Stories

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.112
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill a dot plot for the given newborn-baby weights of boys and girls, then analyse and compare the data.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 13.2 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the dot plots and central-tendency measures of another Grade 5 section, share observations and compare the heights of the two sections.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 13.2 p.113
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given weights of sumo wrestlers and ballet dancers, estimate approximately how many times heavier a sumo wrestler is than a ballet dancer.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the chapter’s height data split into boys and girls and the ‘zero median but high total’ cricket example from section 13.2. Ask: what does it mean when the mean and the median are far apart? Elicit that an outlier pulls the mean but leaves the median nearly unchanged. Students state, in their own words, one situation where the mean is more useful and one where the median is more useful.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.112 (“Fill a dot plot for the given newborn-baby weights of boys and girls, then analyse and compare”), constructing the dot plot and computing mean and median for each group. Comparison questions are answered in writing.

Pairs tackle Figure it Out Q6, section 13.2 p.113 (“From the dot plots and central-tendency measures of another Grade 5 section, share observations and compare”) and Figure it Out Q7, section 13.2 p.113 (“Given weights of sumo wrestlers and ballet dancers, estimate how many times heavier”). For Q7, students must reason from mean weights rather than a formula — prompt: what does ‘about how many times’ require?

Class shares conclusions. Consolidate the outlier principle: a high outlier gives mean > median; a low outlier gives mean < median. Students write one sentence explaining which measure they would report for the newborn-weight data and why.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat the sumo-versus-ballet question as requiring exact division. Encourage estimation using mean weights: the reasoning, not the precise arithmetic, is what the question trains. Watch also for students who report the mean without noting the outlier’s influence — use the newborn data to make this visible on the dot plot.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.3 p.122
textbook_items_in_class.description: From an animal-speed infographic: (a) state the scale; (b) note what is interesting; (c) find a pair where one speed is about twice the other; (d) judge whether a sailfish is about 4 times faster than a humpback whale and the fastest aquatic animal.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.3 p.124
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the superpower-preference responses of Grade 5 and Grade 9, draw a double-bar graph comparing the two grades' choices with an appropriate scale.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 13.3 p.124
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the two-day temperature data for Jodhpur, draw a double-bar graph with scale 1 unit = 4°C and guess the two months.

time_bands.activity: Show the idea of a clustered (double) bar graph by combining two single-column onion-price graphs into one, as described in section 13.3. State the two-step reading process: first identify what is given (organisation, scale, patterns), then infer from what is given (analyse and interpret). Apply these two steps aloud to the rocket-launch graph from section 13.3.

Students read Figure it Out Q1, section 13.3 p.122 (“From an animal-speed infographic: (a) state the scale; (b) note what is interesting; (c) find a pair where one speed is about twice the other; (d) judge whether a sailfish is about 4 times faster…”). Discuss how to judge ‘about 4 times’ from a bar graph — estimation and scale reading, not exact calculation.

Students construct the double-bar graph for Figure it Out Q2, section 13.3 p.124 (“Superpower-preference responses of Grade 5 and Grade 9… choose an appropriate scale”). Emphasise scale choice: the scale must fit all values without leaving most bars tiny. Discuss why colour or pattern fills matter for greyscale readability.

Students begin Figure it Out Q3, section 13.3 p.124 (“Two-day temperature data for Jodhpur… scale 1 unit = 4°C and guess the two months”). After drawing, they write a guess for the months and one sentence of reasoning from the graph’s pattern.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error when constructing double-bar graphs is using different scales for the two bars of the same pair — insist that one shared vertical axis and one scale apply to both datasets. Also remind students that for categories without a natural order (organisations, superpower choices) no time-based left-to-right ordering is imposed, whereas months should follow calendar order.
materials: Coloured pencils or pencils for pattern fills

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.3 p.124–125
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the clustered-bar graph of electric-vehicle registrations: mark the Gujarat and Delhi bars from the table, describe changes 2022–2024, and answer comparison questions about several states.

time_bands.activity: Using the monthly daylight-hour graph for Helsinki and Wellington from section 13.3, apply the two-step process: what is given (months on the x-axis, hours on the y-axis, two bar series) and what can be inferred (the patterns are inverted because the cities are in opposite hemispheres). Ask students to propose a second inference the graph supports and one it does not.

Students work in groups on Figure it Out Q4, section 13.3 p.124–125 (“From the clustered-bar graph of electric-vehicle registrations: mark the Gujarat and Delhi bars, describe changes 2022–2024, answer comparison questions”). Each group divides: one pair marks the bars, another pair reads and answers the comparison questions. Groups then cross-check.

Groups present two conclusions from the EV graph: one supported clearly by the data (a specific comparison with numbers cited) and one that would require additional data (e.g., a claim about national trends from a few states). The class discusses what makes a conclusion ‘graph-supported’.
Brief consolidation: students name one design choice from section 13.3 (colour/pattern for greyscale, time-order for months) and explain why it matters for reading the graph correctly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often treat graph-reading as retrieving plotted values, not reasoning from patterns. The Helsinki–Wellington inversion is a strong example to use: the inference (opposite hemispheres) cannot be read off the scale — it must be argued from the pattern. Push groups to cite specific numbers when they claim a conclusion is ‘graph-supported’.

periods.activity_title: What Does the Data Actually Say?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.4 p.129
textbook_items_in_class.description: From the pocket-count dot plots for boys and girls, decide which statements about variability, median, mean, and maximum are true.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 13.4 p.129–130
textbook_items_in_class.description: From a table of points over four games with a 'did not play' entry: (a) find A's average per game; (b) decide whether to divide C's and B's totals by 3 or 4 and why; (c) decide who is the best performer.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare two groups' General Knowledge quiz scores using mean and median and describe their performance.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the Data Detective theme from section 13.4: comparing boy and girl heights across grades, and the 1989–2019 Indian height survey. Ask: how do we decide whether a claim about the data is justified? Students discuss in pairs: what would make you trust or doubt a statistical claim?

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q1, section 13.4 p.129 (“From the pocket-count dot plots for boys and girls, decide which statements about variability, median, mean, and maximum are true”). After individual work, pairs compare answers and must agree on a final verdict with a one-sentence justification for each statement.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 13.4 p.129–130 (“From a table of points over four games with a ‘did not play’ entry…”). This item centres on the chapter’s zero-versus-no-value distinction: deciding whether to divide by 3 or 4 for players who did not play in one game. Students write out their reasoning before computing.

Pairs share their reasoning for Q2 part (b). Consolidate: not-playing means a value does not exist for that game; dividing by the number of games played gives the correct average. Students then begin Figure it Out Q3, section 13.4 p.130 (“Compare two groups’ General Knowledge quiz scores using mean and median”) as a bridge into the next task.

periods.teacher_notes: The ‘did not play’ question is the sharpest test of whether students understand the mean’s denominator. A common error is dividing by the total number of games for all players, ignoring absences. Tie this explicitly to the chapter’s mango-tree off-season example: months with no flowers should not enter the count when the question is about blooming months.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: From survey data of watching vs participating in five sports, choose a scale, draw a double-bar graph, and write observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: For 17 students' heights, suggest a threshold height that splits the class into two equal groups, and estimate their age from the 'Telling Tall Tales' table.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 13.4 p.130
textbook_items_in_class.description: Two 7th-grade sections each have 15 boys and 15 girls; given one section's mean height is 154.2 cm, choose what must be true about the other section's mean.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 13.4 p.130
homework.description: Describe the mean and median of your class's heights, visualising them on a dot plot.

time_bands.activity: Students construct the double-bar graph for Figure it Out Q4, section 13.4 p.130 (“From survey data of watching vs participating in five sports, choose a scale, draw a double-bar graph, and write observations”). Scale choice is deliberate: students write their chosen scale and justify it before drawing. Each student writes at least two observations below the graph.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q5, section 13.4 p.130 (“For 17 students’ heights, suggest a threshold height that splits the class into two equal groups, and estimate their age from the Telling Tall Tales table”). This requires sorting the heights mentally or on paper, finding the median, and using the survey table as a reference — an application of the measures of central tendency developed in section 13.2 to a section 13.4 context.

Students reason through Figure it Out Q7, section 13.4 p.130 (“Two 7th-grade sections, each 15 boys and 15 girls; one section’s mean is 154.2 cm — what must be true about the other?”). This is a reasoning-under-constraint task: students must decide which option follows necessarily from the mean’s definition without knowing the other section’s data. Pairs discuss before choosing.

Class compares answers for Q7 and identifies which options are possible but not certain vs which must be true. Consolidate: the mean constrains the sum of values (sum = mean × count), and this constraint is what allows deductions about related datasets.

periods.teacher_notes: Students approaching Q5 sometimes pick the threshold arbitrarily rather than linking it to the median as a natural splitting point. Ask: which value leaves exactly as many students above as below it? For Q7, the error is confusing ‘could be true’ with ‘must be true’ — push students to find a counterexample for any option they accept too quickly.

periods.activity_title: Investigating Real Data: Projects and Deductions

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 13.4 p.131
textbook_items_in_class.description: From a skyscraper infographic: (a) estimate the number of skyscrapers in New York, Tokyo, and London; (b) judge the validity of statements about cities relative to Mumbai and the world's tallest building.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 13.4 p.132
textbook_items_in_class.description: For Aditi's Sudoku-solving times over two weeks: (a) construct a dot plot for both weeks; (b) describe the mean, median, and observations.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 13.4 p.133
textbook_items_in_class.description: Small-group project: either 'Our heights vs. our family's heights' (dot plot and double-bar graph of student and family heights) or 'Estimating time' (dot plots and double-bar graph of 1-minute and 3-minute estimates), then pool and analyse everyone's data.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 13.4 p.132–133
homework.description: Individual project: either 'How Long is a Sentence?' (dot-plot sentence lengths from two textbook pages and compare with mean/median) or 'What is in a Name?' (mean/median name length, popular starting letters, median starting letter, and a double-bar graph of vowel/consonant patterns).

time_bands.activity: Students read Figure it Out Q8, section 13.4 p.131 (“From a skyscraper infographic: estimate skyscrapers in New York, Tokyo, London; judge validity of statements about cities relative to Mumbai”). Apply the two-step reading process from section 13.3: what is given, then what can be inferred. Students write verdicts on each statement with a brief justification.

Students work individually on Figure it Out Q10, section 13.4 p.132 (“Aditi’s Sudoku-solving times over two weeks: construct a dot plot for both weeks, describe the mean, median, and observations”). Dot plots are drawn on squared paper. Students then compute mean and median for each week and write two observations comparing the weeks.

Small groups tackle Figure it Out Q13, section 13.4 p.133 (“Either ‘Our heights vs our family’s heights’ or ‘Estimating time’— dot plot and double-bar graph, then pool and analyse everyone’s data”). Groups choose one option and collect, plot, and describe their data within the sitting, then share one finding with the class in the closing segment.

Each group states one conclusion from their project data and identifies whether it is a claim the data supports, or a claim that would need more data to confirm. The class closes with the chapter’s framing: data reveals patterns, but generalisation requires caution.

periods.teacher_notes: For the skyscraper infographic, students sometimes accept visual impressions as proof — push them to cite a number read from the graph before accepting any verdict as ‘graph-supported’. For the group project, remind students that collecting heights or time estimates within this sitting is feasible; pooling and describing the class’s data is more valuable than a polished individual product.
materials: Measuring tape (if heights project is chosen)

items.prompt: Which of the following is a statistical question?

options.label: A
options.text: How many legs does a spider have?

options.label: B
options.text: How many hours do students in our school sleep each night?

options.label: C
options.text: What is the capital of India?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — How many hours do students in our school sleep each night? This is a statistical question because answers vary across students and data must be collected and analysed to draw a conclusion.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition: a statistical question expects variation in answers and requires data to be gathered and analysed.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think any question about a living thing is statistical; this question has a single fixed answer and no variation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be confusing a factual question with a statistical one; the capital of India is a single fixed fact.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be associating numbers with statistics; a arithmetic computation has one correct answer and requires no data collection.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the section 13.1 definition and ask: does this question expect different answers from different people?
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write one more statistical question and one more non-statistical question of their own, and explain the difference in a sentence.

exercise.description: Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball in India; (b) ages of dogs on this street; (c) fraction of the class who like walking up a hill; (d) do you like reading; (e) approximately how many bricks are in this wall; (f) best bowler in yesterday's match; (g) last year's rainfall pattern in Barmer.

items.prompt: A plant produced the following number of flowers on seven consecutive days: 4, 7, 3, 6, 5, 7, 3. Calculate the arithmetic mean number of flowers per day. Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the arithmetic mean formula: sum of all values divided by the number of values.

inclusivity.support: Draw seven boxes, write one value in each, and redistribute the counts equally — the fair-share picture from the chapter makes the mean concrete.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to decide whether the mean is a good representative value for this dataset and to explain in one sentence what happens to the mean if one day had 0 flowers.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.101
exercise.description: Shreyas bounces a ball on a bat with counts 6, 2, 9, 5, 4, 6, 3, 5 over 8 attempts; calculate the average number of bounces.

items.prompt: The prices of tomatoes (in rupees per kg) recorded over nine days are: 18, 22, 19, 25, 21, 18, 24, 20, 22. Sort the values and find the median price.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Sorted: 18, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 22, 24, 25. There are 9 values, so the median is the 5th value = 21 rupees per kg.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sort the data in ascending order and identify the middle value (position = (n + 1) ÷ 2 for odd n).

inclusivity.support: Provide a number line and ask the student to place each value on it before identifying the middle position.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if a 10th day recorded a price of 40 rupees (a high outlier), would the mean or the median change more, and why?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.2 p.112
exercise.description: Find the median of the onion prices in Yahapur and in Wahapur.

items.prompt: A student says: 'How many pages are in our science textbook?' is a statistical question because it involves counting. Is the student correct? Explain using the definition of a statistical question.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is not correct. A statistical question requires that answers vary across observations and that data must be collected and analysed to draw a conclusion. The number of pages in a particular science textbook is a single fixed fact — every copy has the same answer — so no data collection or analysis of variation is needed. It is not a statistical question.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the chapter's criterion: a statistical question expects variation in answers and requires data gathering and analysis.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to talk through the answer with a partner before writing — pair-share helps make the reasoning about variation explicit.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: rewrite the page-count question as a genuinely statistical question, and explain what data you would need to collect.

exercise.description: Decide which of the following are statistical questions: (a) price of a tennis ball in India; (b) ages of dogs on this street; (c) fraction of the class who like walking up a hill; (d) do you like reading; (e) approximately how many bricks are in this wall; (f) best bowler in yesterday's match; (g) last year's rainfall pattern in Barmer.

items.prompt: Eight students recorded how long (in minutes) they spent reading on a particular day: 20, 15, 30, 25, 20, 18, 60, 22. The mean reading time is 26.25 minutes and the median is 21 minutes. Explain why the mean is greater than the median for this dataset, and which measure better represents a typical student's reading time.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The value 60 minutes is an outlier — it is much higher than the rest of the data. An outlier pulls the mean upward, so the mean (26.25 min) is greater than the median (21 min). The median is a better representative of a typical student's reading time because it is not affected by the outlier; most students read for between 15 and 30 minutes, which is close to 21 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the chapter's outlier principle: a high outlier pulls the mean above the median, making the median the more robust representative.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to sketch a dot plot of the values and visually locate where 26.25 and 21 sit relative to most of the dots.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what value would the outlier need to be changed to in order for the mean and median to be equal? Reason through it without necessarily computing exactly.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 13.2 p.112
exercise.description: Fill a dot plot for the given newborn-baby weights of boys and girls, then analyse and compare the data.

items.prompt: A double-bar graph shows the average monthly rainfall (in mm) for two cities — one in the northern hemisphere and one in the southern hemisphere — across all 12 months. A student notices that the bars for the two cities show opposite peaks: when one city has its highest rainfall months, the other has its lowest. What can the student conclude from this pattern, and what would they need to check before generalising this conclusion?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student can conclude that the two cities experience their wet and dry seasons at opposite times of the year, which is consistent with them being in opposite hemispheres — one has summer while the other has winter. Before generalising, the student should check: (1) whether the graph's scale is the same for both cities so the comparison is fair, and (2) that the graph covers all 12 months in calendar order, since the two-step process from section 13.3 requires confirming what is given before inferring from what is given.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the two-step graph-reading process: identify what is given (scale, organisation, pattern) before making an inference about the cause of the pattern.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student of the Helsinki–Wellington daylight-hour example from section 13.3 as a parallel case to use as a thinking scaffold.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what if both cities are in the same hemisphere but at very different latitudes — would the same inverted pattern still be expected? What other graph feature would help distinguish the two explanations?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 13.3 p.124–125
exercise.description: From the clustered-bar graph of electric-vehicle registrations: mark the Gujarat and Delhi bars from the table, describe changes 2022–2024, and answer comparison questions about several states.

items.prompt: In a quiz competition, four students played across three rounds. Student P scored 8, 12, and 10. Student Q scored 15, 0, and 9 (the 0 was because Q arrived late and was not allowed to play that round). A classmate says: 'Q's total is 24, the same as P's total, so they performed equally well.' Do you agree? Justify your answer using the idea of the arithmetic mean and the chapter's distinction between a zero score and not playing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The classmate is not correct. P played three rounds: mean = (8 + 12 + 10) ÷ 3 = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 points per round. Q did not play one round; that round should not be counted. Q's mean = (15 + 9) ÷ 2 = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 points per round played. Comparing totals is misleading because the players played different numbers of rounds — the same problem as comparing cricketers across series of different lengths. Using the mean per round played, Q performed better. The chapter distinguishes a zero score (the player was present and scored nothing) from not playing (no value exists for that round); only the rounds actually played enter the mean's denominator.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the mean-as-fair-representative principle and the zero-versus-no-value distinction: only rounds played enter the denominator.

inclusivity.support: Pair-share: ask the student to explain aloud what the denominator of the mean represents before writing the answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if Q had scored 0 in that round (present but scored nothing), would the conclusion change? Calculate and explain.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.4 p.129
exercise.description: From the pocket-count dot plots for boys and girls, decide which statements about variability, median, mean, and maximum are true.

items.prompt:
The table below shows the number of bicycles sold by two shops — ShopA and ShopB — in each of four months.

Use a scale of 1 unit = 10 bicycles. Calculate the total bicycles sold by each shop across all four months and find the mean monthly sales for each shop.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Month | ShopA | ShopB |
| January | 40 | 30 |
| February | 50 | 60 |
| March | 30 | 50 |
| April | 60 | 40 |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: ShopA total = 40 + 50 + 30 + 60 = 180 bicycles; mean = 180 ÷ 4 = 45 bicycles per month. ShopB total = 30 + 60 + 50 + 40 = 180 bicycles; mean = 180 ÷ 4 = 45 bicycles per month. Both shops have the same mean monthly sales despite different month-by-month patterns.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply mean = sum ÷ count to each shop's four monthly values; note that equal means can coexist with different individual patterns.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the double-bar graph first with the given scale to make the totals visible before computing — the visual representation scaffolds the numerical work.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what additional measure (range or minimum/maximum) would distinguish the two shops' performance patterns, given that their means are equal?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 13.3 p.122
exercise.description: From an animal-speed infographic: (a) state the scale; (b) note what is interesting; (c) find a pair where one speed is about twice the other; (d) judge whether a sailfish is about 4 times faster than a humpback whale and the fastest aquatic animal.

items.prompt:
Two groups of six students each completed a maths puzzle. Their times (in minutes) were:
Group X: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13, 15
Group Y: 10, 20, 11, 12, 13, 10

For each group, find (a) the mean time and (b) the median time. Then state which group was more consistent and justify using the range.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: (a) Group X mean = (12+15+11+14+13+15) ÷ 6 = 80 ÷ 6 ≈ 13.3 min. Group Y mean = (10+20+11+12+13+10) ÷ 6 = 76 ÷ 6 ≈ 12.7 min. (b) Group X sorted: 11,12,13,14,15,15 — median = (13+14) ÷ 2 = 13.5 min. Group Y sorted: 10,10,11,12,13,20 — median = (11+12) ÷ 2 = 11.5 min. Range: Group X = 15−11 = 4 min; Group Y = 20−10 = 10 min. Group X is more consistent because its range is smaller — the times are closer together. Group Y has a high outlier (20 min) that widens its range and pulls its mean above its median.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute mean (sum ÷ count) and median (middle of sorted data) for each group; compare range as the measure of variability and consistency.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line for each group and place the values on it to make sorting and locating the median visual before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: if the student who took 20 minutes in Group Y had been absent (not playing), how would the mean and median of Group Y change?

items.prompt: A data detective reads the following claim: 'Students in Section A of Grade 7 are taller on average than students in Section B, so Grade 7 students at this school are taller than at all other schools in the district.' Identify one conclusion that can be supported by the data described, and one that cannot be supported. Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Supported conclusion: Section A's mean height is greater than Section B's mean height — this follows directly from the data collected for those two sections. Not supported: claiming Grade 7 students at this school are taller than at all other schools in the district. The data covers only two sections in one school; drawing a conclusion about the whole district would require collecting and comparing data from all schools in the district. As section 13.4 cautions, one or two schools' data cannot be generalised to a wider population.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the data-detective principle from section 13.4: separate claims the data directly supports from those requiring broader data collection.

inclusivity.support: Use an alternate representation: list what data was actually collected (Section A and B heights at one school) and ask what questions that data can and cannot answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask: what additional data would you need to collect to make the district-wide claim valid, and how would you collect it fairly?
